question.text: Given that $g(x,y)=y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} &= \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} + \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}r\sin\theta + \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}r\cos\theta . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} =0,\qquad \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} = 2y \end{align}

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= 0, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= 2r\sin\theta. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} &= 0\,(-r\sin\theta) + (2r\sin\theta) \,r \cos \theta \\[5pt] & = r^2\sin(2\theta) . \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $g(x,y)=\ln (x+y),$ find $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial r} &= \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial r} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}\cos\theta + \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}\sin\theta . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} = \dfrac 1 {x+y},\qquad \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} = \dfrac 1 {x+y} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac 1 {r\cos\theta+r\sin\theta}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac 1 {r\cos\theta+r\sin\theta}. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial r} &= \left(\dfrac 1 {r\cos\theta+r\sin\theta}\right)\cos\theta + \left(\dfrac 1 {r\cos\theta+r\sin\theta}\right)\sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cos\theta + \sin\theta}{r(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{r} . \end{align}

question.text: Given that $q(x,y)=xy,$ find $\dfrac{\partial q}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $q(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial \theta} &= \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} + \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\partial q}{\partial x}r\sin\theta + \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial y}r\cos\theta . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $q$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial x} =y,\qquad \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial y} = x \end{align}

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial x} &= r\sin\theta, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial y} &= r\cos\theta. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial q}{\partial \theta} &= -(r\sin\theta)\, r \sin\theta + (r\cos\theta) \,r \cos \theta \\[5pt] & = -r^2\sin^2\theta + r^2\cos^2\theta \\[5pt] & = r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta) \\[5pt] & = r^2\cos(2\theta) . \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $w(x,y)=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{y^2}{2},$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta} &= \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} + \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}r\sin\theta + \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y}r\cos\theta . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} =x,\qquad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} = y \end{align}

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} &= r\cos\theta, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} &= r\sin\theta. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta} &=- (r\cos\theta)\,r\sin\theta + (r\sin\theta) \,r\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= -r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta + r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $f(x,y)=2xy+y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}r\sin\theta + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}r\cos\theta . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ \begin{align} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} =2y,\qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2x+2y \end{align}

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= 2r\sin\theta, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= 2r\cos\theta+2r\sin\theta. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} &= -2r \sin \theta \, r \sin \theta + (2r \cos \theta+2r \sin \theta) r \cos \theta \\[5pt] & = 2r^2( \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) +r^2 \sin (2\theta) \\[5pt] & = 2r^2 \cos (2 \theta) +r^2 \sin (2\theta) . \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $h(r, \theta)=r(\cos \theta-1),$ find $\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

\[ \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial r} = \cos\theta - 1, \qquad \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial \theta} = -r\sin \theta \end{align*}

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} &= \left(\cos\theta-1\right)\cos\theta - \dfrac1r\left(-r\sin \theta\right)\sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \cos^2\theta - \cos\theta + \sin^2\theta \\[5pt] &= 1-\cos\theta. \end{align}

question.text: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r\cos2\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

\[ \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\sin\theta + \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\cos\theta. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r} = \cos 2\theta, \qquad \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta} = -2r\sin2\theta \end{align*}

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} &= \left(\cos2\theta\right)\sin\theta + \dfrac1r\left(-2r\sin2\theta\right)\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \cos 2\theta\sin\theta - 2\cos\theta\sin2\theta. \end{align}

question.text: Given that $v(r, \theta)=r(1 + \cos 2\theta),$ find $\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

\[ \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial r}\sin\theta + \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial \theta}\cos\theta. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial r} = 1 + \cos 2\theta, \qquad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial \theta} = -2r\sin 2\theta \end{align*}

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} &= \left(1 + \cos 2\theta\right)\sin\theta + \dfrac1r\left(-2r\sin 2\theta\right)\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos2\theta - 2\cos\theta\sin2\theta . \end{align}

question.text: Given that $v(r, \theta)=r^2 + 2r\cos\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

\[ \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial r} = 2r + 2\cos\theta, \qquad \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial \theta} = -2r\sin \theta \end{align*}

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} &= \left(2r + 2\cos\theta\right)\cos\theta - \dfrac1r\left(-2r\sin \theta\right)\sin\theta \\[5pt] &= 2r\cos\theta + 2\cos^2\theta + 2\sin^2\theta \\[5pt] &= 2r\cos\theta + 2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) \\[5pt] &= 2r\cos\theta + 2. \end{align}

question.text: Given that $g(r, \theta)=r^2\cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

\[ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial r}\sin\theta + \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial \theta}\cos\theta. \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial r} = 2r\cos 3\theta, \qquad \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} = -3r^2\sin3\theta \end{align*}

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \left(2r\cos3\theta\right)\sin\theta + \dfrac1r\left(-3r^2\sin3\theta\right)\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= r \left(2\sin\theta\cos3\theta - 3\cos\theta\sin3\theta\right) . \end{align}

question.text: Given that $f(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+2yz,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}r\sin\theta + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}r\cos\theta . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y+2z%, %\qquad %\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = 2y \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= 2r\cos\theta, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= 2r\sin\theta+2z. \\[5pt] %\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} &= 2r\sin\theta. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} &= -(2r\cos\theta)r\sin\theta + (2r\sin\theta+2z)r\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= -2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta + 2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta+2rz\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 2rz\cos\theta . \end{align}

question.text: Given that $g(x,y,z)=x^2z+z^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z} . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $z{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z} = x^2+2z \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z} &= r^2\cos^2\theta + 2z. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $u(x,y,z)=x^2z^2+x^2y^2+xyz,$ find $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $u(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $z{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} = 2x^2z+xy \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} &= 2r^2z\cos^2\theta + r^2\cos\theta \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= r^2\left(2z\cos^2\theta + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin2\theta\right) . \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $h(x,y,z)=2x^2+y^2+4x^2z^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.explanation:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

\begin{align} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial z} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} . \end{align}

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $z{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} = 8x^2z \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} &= 8r^2z\cos^2\theta. \end{align*}
